newsitem.title: CANADA: Midland Walwyn seeks banking role.
newsitem.headline: Midland Walwyn seeks banking role.

text.p: Midland Walwyn Inc, Canada's last big independent brokerage, wants to expand into banking, Chief Executive Robert Schultz told Reuters.

Schultz said in an interview this week that he would like Midland to be part of the Interac bank machine system and for the federal government to allow Midland direct access to Canada's check-clearing system.
"We think we're a significant enough financial institution that we should have that access and we should be able to provide banking services to our clients," Schultz said.

Only 12 financial institutions have access to check-clearing in Canada. They include Canada's six major banks, a provincially owned set of treasury branches, some second-tier banks and a trust company. Other financial institutions must have their checks cleared through them.
Schultz also said that he believed Midland could remain independent, although most other Canadian brokerages have been gobbled up by the banks.
He added that Midland itself could be looking for acquisitions in Canada and the United States.

"We've been looking at doing an acquisition of an asset management business," Schultz said. "There are some very good niche players and certain ones might make sense for us if they have any interest in doing something and certainly at some point in time we may have to look south of the border."

He said a key takeover defense for Midland was its 1,200 financial advisers and planners who hold about 20 percent of Midland stock. He said any potential suitor would need to convince Midland's employees to tender their shares and keep working for the company.
Midland's book value is about C$8.80 a share or C$323 million, based on 36.7 million shares .

Schultz said a takeover at 1.6 times book value, such as Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce's proposed US$525 million acquisition this week of Wall Street brokerage Oppenheimer & Co, would cost about C$517 million.
"You're not going to put that money on the table unless all the assets are going to be in line," Schultz said.
Earlier this week, Midland said its second-quarter earnings rose to C$17.4 million or C$0.46 a share from year earlier C$10.4 million or C$0.28 a share.
Schultz expects Midland to exceed its goals for this year set out in its 1996 annual report.
That would include exceeding a targeted return on equity of 20 percent and increasing client assets under administration to more than C$44 billion from C$34.6 billion.
